explanations: terra: People are commanded to worship their Lord who created them and those before them, setting up the rain, fruit, and provision detailed in 2:22.

luna: The section depicts land receiving rain and producing provision, then the human forgetting its giver. This ayah says God made the earth a resting place, sent down water, and brought forth fruits as provision, before warning against setting up rivals to Him. | terra: The Lord creates people, makes earth and sky serviceable, and sends rain that produces fruits as provision; recipients are told not to give His place to rivals.

luna: The section’s K-N-D dictionary gloss includes refusing continued closeness. This ayah describes people who break God’s covenant and cut what He ordered to be joined, giving the severed bond a communal and moral form. | terra: Those who break God's covenant after its binding and cut what He commanded joined enact the severing that the section pictures as a cut cord of gratitude.
terra: Water springs from rock for the tribes, who are told to eat and drink God's provision without corrupting earth.
terra: The described cow has not been trained تُثِيرُ ٱلْأَرْضَ or water a field, preserving the source section's secondary use of the same root for plowing.
terra: Abraham asks his Lord to make the city secure and provide its believing people with fruits, locating produce and safety in lordly provision.
terra: God speaks of completing His favor so that people may be guided, another direct use of completed bounty as an aim of care.
terra: “Remember Me, I will remember you” makes the relation reciprocal, then commands gratitude and forbids ingratitude; it is the uncut version of the section's two-way cord.

luna: The section assembles wind, cloud, water, and earth into a chain of care. This ayah places the winds, clouds, rain, and revived earth together among God’s signs, with a concluding call to reason; it lets the reader see the whole field relation at once. | terra: Rain revives earth, creatures spread, winds turn, and cloud is held between heaven and earth; this lays out the field's whole administered ecology.

luna: The section says the receiver cuts the return of thanks to the giver. This ayah tells believers to eat the good provisions God gave them and be grateful to Him, directly naming the reciprocal response. | terra: Believers are told to eat the good things God provided and thank Him if they worship Him, directly binding consumed provision to gratitude.

luna: The section links love of خير with gratitude and maintaining a bond. This ayah describes righteousness as giving beloved wealth to relatives, orphans, and the needy, while keeping promises; it joins generosity to sustained obligations. | terra: True righteousness includes giving wealth despite one's love for it, turning حُبّ of possession into an onward gift rather than kenud withholding.
terra: A person who leaves خَيْر is instructed about a bequest; here the named word carries the wealth sense rather than the section's gift sense.

luna: The section’s Rab gloss includes the one who improves, while kenūd land bears no growth. This ayah depicts a person who spreads corruption and destroys crops and offspring, a human reversal of the Rabb’s nurturing work. | terra: When the corrupt person turns away he destroys crops and livestock, actively undoing the nurturing field system rather than merely failing to yield.
terra: The answer to what should be spent calls it خَيْر and directs it to relatives and vulnerable recipients, using the named word in an explicitly generous sense.

terra: Wives are called a tilth, bringing marital relation and soil into one metaphor; the link to the source's separate “woman who does not maintain connection” and “non-growing earth” senses remains indirect.
terra: One who rejects false masters and believes in God grasps the firmest handhold that has no break, a positive boundary against the cut cord of gratitude.

luna: The section names grain (حبة) and says a good yield is the expected return of care. This ayah compares a charitable gift to a seed grain producing seven ears, joining crop and generosity as multiplied return. | terra: Spending in God's way is a grain that grows seven ears and manifold seed, turning a passed-on gift into cultivated abundance.
terra: Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminders or injury preserve its benefit, the relational condition illustrated by the soils in 2:264-265.

luna: The section’s kenūd soil yields nothing despite rain. This ayah compares showy or injurious giving to a smooth rock with a thin covering of soil that rain leaves bare, making failed generosity resemble a field unable to retain its yield. | terra: A gift spoiled by reproach is like soil on smooth rock stripped bare by rain; giving whose relation is cut produces nothing.

luna: The section’s good-soil image is paired here with spending for God’s approval: a garden on a height receives rain and yields twice over. It shows a generous response taking root in receptive ground. | terra: Sincere spending is a garden whose rain doubles its yield and whose drizzle still suffices, the fruitful opposite of both 2:264 and kenud soil.

luna: The section’s field image presents a cultivated yield as a gift that can be lost. This ayah pictures a garden destroyed by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is old and dependent, making the security of provision fragile. | terra: A fruiting garden with rivers and every produce is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is vulnerable, exposing the boundary of assumed possession.

luna: The section names grain as the expected yield and خير as gift or generosity. This ayah tells people to spend from the good things they earn and from what God brings forth from the earth, joining harvest to a generous return.
terra: Whatever خَيْر people spend is for their own good and will be repaid fully, describing gift as a continuing rather than severed relation.
terra: God makes charity grow while effacing usury and does not love any persistent ingrate; growth through generous giving is set against kafur.
terra: Love of accumulated wealth, fine horses, livestock, and tilled land is made alluring; the list gives concrete forms to severe love of al-khayr.
terra: God is addressed as owner of dominion who gives and removes rule, while all ٱلْخَيْرُ is in His hand; ownership and good-as-gift meet.
terra: Whether what is within breasts is hidden or disclosed, God knows it, supporting the section's Lord informed of concealed inner contents.
terra: Mary's Lord accepts her graciously and makes her grow with a good growth, using plant language for the section's gradual divine nurture.
terra: People are told to be rabbāniyyūn through teaching and studying scripture, a derivative of the named root that joins disciplined formation to divine learning.

luna: The section says a person loves خير, which its dictionary entry glosses as gift and generosity. This ayah says righteousness is not attained until one spends what one loves; it turns attachment to good into a response of giving. | terra: People do not attain full goodness until they give from what they love, turning intense attachment to a gift into generosity.
terra: Holding God's rope is joined to remembering His favor and the bond He made between formerly hostile hearts, a direct positive form of the section's cut favor-cord.
terra: The spending of wrongdoers is like a freezing wind destroying a crop; cultivated value becomes non-yield through their own wrongdoing.
terra: Good received is from God, while evil that befalls is from oneself, and God suffices as witness; this corrects the kenud habit of remembering harms but losing their gifts' source.

luna: The section depicts ingratitude toward the Rabb as a broken response. This ayah asks what God would gain by punishing people if they are grateful and believe, stating the significance of the response without the section’s field imagery.

luna: The section says a blessing can be brought to completion through Rabb-like care. This ayah says God completed His favor and perfected the religion that day, giving completion of favor a direct Qur’anic formulation. | terra: Completion of religion and favor is announced together, preserving the source section's definition of a benefit brought to completion.
terra: Purification is explained as God's desire to complete His favor so that people may be grateful, using the exact completion-of-bounty sense developed for Rabb.
terra: Earlier peoples received abundant rain and flowing rivers but were destroyed for their sins and replaced, showing plentiful water as care that does not excuse refusal.

luna: The section connects the Rabb’s knowledge to the field’s grain and leaves. This ayah says no leaf falls without God knowing it and mentions a grain in the darkness of earth; the same growth scene remains fully within divine knowledge. | terra: God knows every leaf that falls and every grain, حَبَّةٍ, in earth's darkness, joining the field's seed to complete knowledge of what is hidden.
terra: People promise gratitude if God rescues them from dangers of land and sea, explicitly voicing the return owed for deliverance.
terra: God rescues them from every distress, yet they associate partners again; the promised gratitude of 6:63 is severed.

luna: The section names grain in its ح ب ب dictionary entry and describes soil’s failure to produce. This ayah says God splits the grain and date-stone and brings the living from the dead, locating crop and renewed life in the same act.

luna: The section’s wheat-and-barley grain gloss and rain-fed field are both present here: water descends, plants grow, and grain, dates, grapes, and olives appear. The abundance shows what the kenūd land refuses to yield. | terra: Water from the sky produces vegetation and clustered grain, giving another direct formulation of the cloud-to-grain sequence.

luna: The section describes harvested grain and care of the land. This ayah says to eat the crop when it bears fruit and give its due on harvest day, linking yield with a return to others. | terra: At harvest people must give the crop's due and avoid excess, making a tended field the source of an onward gift rather than possession alone.
terra: The speaker asks whether any lord besides God should be sought when He is the Lord of everything, closely matching the source definition “the rabb of each thing is its owner.”
luna: The section describes land sustaining a person while the person is kenūd to the Rabb. This ayah says God established people on earth and provided means of livelihood, then says few give thanks.

luna: The section describes Rabb as the one who repairs and land as the recipient of nurturing. This ayah forbids corruption after the earth has been set right and says God’s mercy is near to those who do good, reversing the kenūd refusal of care.

luna: The section’s field chain begins with wind and rain reaching dead land. This ayah says the winds carry heavy clouds to a dead land, where water brings forth fruits; it supplies the rain-to-yield movement immediately before the soil contrast in 7:58. | terra: The winds carry a heavy cloud to dead land, water descends, and fruits emerge; this is the nurturing sequence whose two soils are distinguished in 7:58.

luna: The section quotes this soil comparison: good land brings forth its plants by its Lord’s permission, while corrupt land yields only sparingly; the ending addresses those who give thanks. It makes the barren kenūd soil an image of a response that withholds what care could produce. | terra: Good soil yields by its Lord's permission, bad soil yields only scant growth, and the ayah closes with gratitude; this states the section's fertile-versus-kanud earth image almost whole.

luna: The section allows 100:7’s witness to refer to the human or to the Rabb. Here God asks “ألست بربكم” and the people answer “شهدنا”; it supplies a remembered testimony to the Rabb as the relation later denied. | terra: God makes humankind testify against themselves to His lordship; Rabb and self-witness meet exactly as the section allows for the pronoun in 100:7.
terra: People are told to remember when they were weak and afraid, then sheltered, strengthened, and given good provision so that they might thank.

luna: The section treats favor as a sustained relation that can be answered or severed. This ayah says God does not change a favor bestowed on a people until they change what is within themselves, making the response part of the relation.
terra: If family, acquired wealth, trade, and dwellings are more loved than God, people must await His command; حُبّ of gifts is measured against their giver.
terra: Taking scholars and monks as lords beside God shows the obeyed-master sense of rabb redirected to improper claimants.

luna: The section describes a person severing gratitude after gifts arrive. This ayah recounts people who promise that if God gives them from His bounty they will give charity and be righteous, making the promised return explicit.

luna: The section says the recipient cuts the return of gratitude. This ayah says that once they receive from God’s bounty, they become stingy and turn away, matching the break between gift and thanks.

luna: The section says the Rabb knows those who fail to honor the bond. This ayah describes the lasting hypocrisy in their hearts after they broke their promise, showing a breach that remains known to God.

luna: The section describes an ingrate who counts distress and forgets blessings. This ayah says a person calls upon God when harm touches him, then passes on as though he had never called once harm is removed, making forgetfulness explicit. | terra: The afflicted human calls God in every posture, then after relief passes on as though he never called, severing remembered need from received rescue.

luna: The section names the human’s ingratitude after distress has passed. This ayah stages people calling to God in a storm at sea; 10:23 supplies the specific post-rescue transgression, while this row contributes the desperate plea.

luna: The section says the person cuts gratitude after receiving care. This ayah says that once God saves people to land they transgress; 10:22 supplies their plea at sea, while this row gives the turning-away response.
terra: Rain makes earth's growth luxuriant until its people think they control it, then God's command leaves it harvested bare; possession forgets the true giver.

luna: The section says those who cut the bond do not leave their Lord’s knowledge. This ayah says no matter what people do, their Lord is witness over them and nothing is hidden from Him, making that claim concrete. | terra: No recitation or deed is undertaken without God witnessing it, and not even an atom's weight escapes the Lord, grounding testimony in complete knowledge.

luna: The section says the human can count loss and forget earlier care. This ayah describes despair when mercy is withdrawn after the person has tasted it, a concrete reversal in how favor is remembered. | terra: When mercy is withdrawn after being tasted, the human becomes despairing and ungrateful, reducing the whole history of care to the present loss.

luna: The section depicts ingratitude to the Rabb after gifts. This ayah describes boastful rejoicing after hardship is removed, showing a human response that treats restored ease as self-evident rather than as care. | terra: When favor follows hardship, the human says the evils have left and becomes exultant and boastful, enjoying the reversal without returning it to the giver.
terra: Seeking the Lord's forgiveness is followed by the promise of abundant rain and added strength, while turning away would sever that renewed relation.

terra: The Lord does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are reformers; this indirectly places Rabb beside iṣlāḥ, one of the source dictionary's lordly senses, without identifying the two roles outright.

luna: The section’s ر ب ب dictionary gloss includes completing a given blessing. This ayah says God will complete His favor upon Joseph and the family of Jacob, naming the same movement from gift to completion. | terra: Joseph's Lord will choose and teach him and complete His favor upon him and Jacob's family, making development itself a divine gift.
terra: Joseph says “he is my rabb and made my lodging good”; whether rabb here denotes God or his human master is disputed, but either reading joins benefaction to refusal to betray the relation.
terra: Joseph tells one prisoner that he will pour wine for his rabb, using the named root in its secondary human-master sense.
terra: Joseph asks the freed prisoner to mention him to his rabb, again using the root for a human master rather than the nurturing divine Lord.
terra: Joseph commands seven years of diligent sowing and keeping the grain in its ears, a concrete farmer-and-grain scene.
terra: Seven hard years consume what was stored except a little, placing scarcity beside the cultivated abundance of 12:47.
terra: A later year brings relief and pressing of produce, restoring yield after the scarcity of 12:48.
terra: Neighboring soils and gardens drink the same water yet differ in produce, clarifying how response can differ despite one common nurture.
terra: God shows lightning in fear and hope and raises heavy clouds, presenting the cloud before its water becomes either hoped-for provision or danger.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for ن ق ع includes floodwater gathering, and its image asks what care yields. This ayah stages rain-fed valleys carrying foam that passes while what benefits people remains; it gives the collected-water image a distinction between transient and lasting yield. | terra: Water descends, valleys carry it according to capacity, and flood bears passing foam while what benefits people remains in earth; this expands the section's pooled floodwater into measured reception.
terra: The people of understanding fulfill God's covenant and do not break the compact, preserving the bond whose breakers appear in 13:25.

luna: The section’s K-N-D dictionary gloss includes refusal to maintain closeness. This ayah praises those who join what God commanded to be joined, a direct contrary pattern to the bond the section says kenūd cuts. | terra: They join what God commands to be joined and fear their Lord, the explicit positive reversal of severing the giver's bond.

luna: The section’s K-N-D gloss includes ingratitude to maintaining a bond. This ayah describes breaking covenant and cutting what God ordered joined; it makes the image of severed reciprocity a concrete breach. | terra: Breaking God's covenant and severing what He commanded joined gives the covenantal form of refusing to maintain the bond.

luna: The section calls gratitude the return that is cut off. This ayah directly contrasts شكر with kufr and says thanks brings increase, giving the severed return a stated consequence. | terra: The Lord promises increase for gratitude and warns of punishment for ingratitude, showing that the receiver's return either continues or breaks bounty.

luna: The section’s image asks what sustained care can make grow, while its kenūd gloss names a cut bond. This ayah compares a good word to a tree with firm roots and high branches, joining rootedness and fruitful speech. | terra: A good word is likened to a good tree with a firm root and high branches, making stable relation visible as rooted growth.

luna: The section says the yield of good soil is what care brings to completion. This ayah says the tree bears fruit by its Lord’s permission in every season, making ongoing yield a picture of granted care. | terra: The good tree gives fruit in every season by its Lord's permission, a verbal and conceptual parallel to the good land of 7:58.

luna: The section describes both a severed gratitude bond and land that bears nothing. This ayah compares a bad word to a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, a direct reversal of rooted, fruitful continuity. | terra: A bad word is like a bad tree uprooted from earth with no stability, the non-rooting counterpart to the fruitful tree of 14:24-25.
terra: God sends water from the sky, brings forth fruits as provision, and subjects ships and rivers; this supplies the cultivated gifts whose uncountability and human ingratitude 14:34 names.
terra: Sun, moon, night, and day are subjected for people, continuing the inventory of gifts that 14:34 says cannot be counted.

luna: The section’s K-N-D dictionary gloss says the ingrate counts afflictions and forgets favors. Here God’s نعمة cannot be counted, yet the human is called unjust and ungrateful; the contrast corrects what a person chooses to count. | terra: The uncountability of God's favor is set against إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَانَ لَظَلُومٌ كَفَّارٌ; it reverses the kenud who counts misfortunes and forgets gifts.
terra: Abraham tells his Lord that he settled descendants in an uncultivated valley, asks for fruit as provision, and states gratitude as the hoped-for response.
terra: The earth is spread and everything is caused to grow there in due balance, describing a field fitted before it yields.
terra: God places livelihoods on earth for people and for creatures they do not provide for, between measured growth in 15:19 and divine stores in 15:21.
terra: The stores of all things are with God and descend only in known measure, identifying the hidden source behind the wind and water of 15:22.

luna: The section’s cloud, rain, and plant scene is named across roots and prose. This ayah says winds are sent as fertilizing and water is sent down, a close parallel to weather sustaining growth. | terra: God sends fertilizing winds, brings water from the sky, and gives it to drink while humans do not control its stores; the whole field system is received.

luna: The section’s cloud-and-field chain turns on rain reaching the earth. This ayah names water sent down from the sky as drink and as the means for pasture and trees to grow, showing how provision starts. | terra: Water from the sky supplies drink and the vegetation on which herds feed, the first movement of the section's nurturing rain.

luna: The section names the grain expected from cared-for soil. This ayah says rain produces crops, olives, palms, grapes, and other fruits; it supplies specific forms of the yield the barren land withholds. | terra: The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits, completing 16:10's movement from rain to yield.
terra: The subjected sea supplies food, ornaments, and travel for seeking God's bounty, and the sequence aims at gratitude.

luna: The section’s K-N-D gloss says the ingrate counts troubles and forgets gifts. This ayah says if people count God’s favors they cannot enumerate them, giving the opposite scale of what is forgotten. | terra: God's favors cannot be counted, preserving the section's reversal of a kenud person who counts harms and forgets benefits.

luna: The section says a person can forget the Rabb behind a gift. This ayah states that every blessing people have is from God, then says they call upon Him in distress; it identifies the giver before the human response. | terra: Every favor people possess is from God, and distress makes them appeal to Him, identifying the giver whom ease later obscures.
terra: Once God removes distress, some assign partners to their Lord, cutting the appeal-to-rescue relation stated in 16:53.
terra: Their partnership is said to deny what God gave them, naming ingratitude as rejection of the gift's source.
terra: God sends water and revives dead earth, a concise direct parallel to land made receptive by rain.

luna: The section calls kenūd ingratitude for the provision one receives. This ayah says people favored with provision do not pass it on to those under their authority and asks whether they deny God’s favor, making withheld sharing a form of denial.

luna: The section’s Rab gloss includes owner and provider. This ayah names spouses, children, and good provision given by God, then asks whether people believe in falsehood and deny His favor; it extends the gift relation from food to family. | terra: Spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision are given by God, yet people believe falsehood and deny God's favor; a whole history of nurture is cut from its giver.

luna: The section says the human forgets gifts while failing to thank their giver. This ayah names hearing, sight, and hearts given to people as they emerge from their mothers, with the purpose that they may be grateful. | terra: God brings people from the womb knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts so that they may thank, a staged gift ordered toward gratitude.

luna: The section’s root gloss associates Rabb with completing a blessing. This ayah says God completes His favor upon people through shade, shelter, and protection, supplying concrete forms of care. | terra: After listing shade, shelter, clothing, and armor, God says He thus completes His favor so that people may submit.
terra: People recognize God's favor and then deny it; knowledge of the gift without preserving its relation to the giver is precisely the section's cut gratitude.
terra: Justice, excellence, and giving to relatives are commanded immediately before covenant keeping in 16:91, joining maintained bonds to onward generosity.
terra: The command not to break confirmed oaths says that God is witness to what people do, combining an unbroken bond with the section's knowing witness.
terra: The woman who unravels her yarn after it was strong supplies a literal cord-image for breaking a confirmed relation, continuing 16:91.

luna: The section’s kenūd person fails to return thanks for nourishment. This town had أمن and رزق from every place, then met the consequence of kufr; the provision and failed response occupy one scene. | terra: A secure town with abundant provision responds to God's favors with ingratitude and is made to taste hunger and fear; provision and kenud are directly opposed.

luna: The section’s خير includes gifts and generosity, and its field scene yields food. This ayah tells people to eat God’s lawful, good provision and thank Him for His favor, joining nourishment to gratitude. | terra: People must eat God's lawful good provision and thank God's favor, stating the response that kenud cuts off.
terra: Abraham is described as grateful for God's favors, chosen, and guided, a personal positive counterpart to kenud.
terra: Night and day allow people to seek the Lord's bounty and calculate years and reckoning, linking provision with rightly directed counting.

luna: The section’s surah context asks whether the human knows what will be exposed after the graves are opened. This ayah says each person’s record is attached to him and brought out on resurrection day, making accountability individual.

luna: The section says the human is witness to his own response. This ayah tells the person to read his record and says he is sufficient as his own reckoner, directly joining self-witness to the record. | terra: At judgment the human is told to read his own record and is sufficient that day as reckoner against himself, a close parallel to self-witness in 100:7.
terra: The prayer “have mercy on them as they raised me when small” uses رَبَّيَانِي for stepwise human nurture and calls for a return of care.
terra: The Lord expands and measures provision with full sight and knowledge of His servants, joining calibrated bounty to divine awareness.

luna: The section says a person cuts the return of gratitude to the giver. This ayah names the human as كفور after God rescues people from distress at sea and they turn away on reaching land, making the severed response concrete. | terra: After God rescues people from danger at sea they turn away, and the human is called ungrateful; the rescue-to-forgetting turn enacts kenud.

luna: The section describes the recipient who forgets the giver after receiving خير. This ayah says a person turns aside when favored but despairs when touched by evil, echoing the section’s contrast between gifts and counted afflictions. | terra: Favor makes the human turn aside while evil makes him despair, the same asymmetric memory of blessing and harm described for kenud.

luna: The section depicts the human as ungrateful to the Rabb and intensely attached to خير. This ayah says that if people possessed the treasures of their Lord’s mercy, they would withhold them for fear of spending, directly naming the stinginess that blocks reciprocity.
terra: The adornment on earth will be made barren ground, a temporal reversal from productive surface to land that yields nothing.

luna: The section’s soil image concerns what land yields under care. This ayah introduces a man given two gardens of grapes, surrounded by palms and crops, a specific instance of received agricultural abundance. | terra: The parable begins with a man given two vineyards surrounded by palms and crops, making cultivated plenty a received gift.
terra: Both gardens yield fully without withholding anything and a river runs between them, the complete opposite of non-producing soil.

luna: The section’s word حبّ names love and خير can mean wealth or gift. This ayah’s garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, turning received abundance into self-regard. | terra: Possessing abundant fruit and wealth leads the owner to boast of being greater, showing bounty being mistaken for self-sufficiency.

luna: The section says a person forgets the giver while clinging to what he has received. This ayah shows the garden owner wronging himself and assuming his garden will never perish, treating provision as secure in itself. | terra: He enters his garden wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, forgetting the giver while loving the gift.

luna: The section’s surah context asks whether the human knows he will be raised and his inward contents exposed. This ayah’s garden owner doubts the Hour and presumes he will receive something better if returned to his Lord, exposing confidence in wealth against accountability. | terra: The garden owner doubts the Hour yet expects an even better return from his Lord, treating Rabb as guarantor of gifts while denying accountability.

luna: The section’s Rab gloss describes one who nurtures and forms through stages. The garden owner’s companion answers that the Lord created him from dust, then a drop, then formed him as a man; it grounds human life in received creation. | terra: His companion recalls the One who created him through stages and challenges his rejection, answering the owner's self-sufficient stance.
terra: The companion declares “He is Allah, my Lord” and refuses partners, restoring the true owner behind the garden.

luna: The section says a recipient forgets the source of his garden-like provision. The companion tells the owner to say “ما شاء الله لا قوة إلا بالله” on entering his garden, giving words for recognizing the giver and one’s dependence. | terra: The owner should have entered saying that what God wills occurs and power belongs to God; this is the missing acknowledgment at receipt of the gift.

luna: The section’s good-soil image can be reversed into a land that fails. This ayah has the companion warn that God may give him a better garden and send a calamity upon the other, making the yield’s dependence on God explicit. | terra: The companion warns that his Lord may give a better garden and send a calamity upon this one, locating both gift and loss under the Rabb.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for ن ق ع includes gathered water and its field depends on rain. This ayah warns that the garden’s water may sink into the earth so its owner cannot recover it, showing how the water that sustains yield is not his possession. | terra: The garden's water may sink so deep that its owner cannot recover it, a boundary to the section's water collecting accessibly in low soil.

luna: The section says the human is ungrateful to his Rabb despite provision. This ayah’s garden owner sees his crop ruined, regrets what he spent, and wishes he had not associated anyone with his Lord; loss makes the forgotten relation visible. | terra: The crop is destroyed and the owner wrings his hands over what he spent, finally regretting the partners he set beside his Lord.

luna: The section says the Rabb remains the one who knows and sustains those who cut the bond. After the garden is destroyed, this ayah says the owner has no group to help him against God, showing the limit of human control over received provision.

luna: The section names Rabb as owner and master. This ayah concludes the garden account by placing true protection with God and the better reward and outcome with Him, restoring the ownership the garden owner ignored.

luna: The section describes rain, soil, and expected growth. This ayah pictures rain-fed vegetation mixing, then drying and scattering as debris, a repeated field image that adds the passing of a crop to the section’s account of provision.

luna: The section’s خير dictionary gloss includes gift and wealth. This ayah calls wealth and children ornaments of worldly life but says enduring good deeds are better with the Lord, distinguishing a received good from what lasts.

luna: The section says the Rabb knows those who cut the gratitude bond and the surah asks what is within graves and chests. This ayah lays out the record and says no small or great deed is left uncounted, making that knowledge exhaustive.

luna: The section’s Rab gloss includes the one who improves and nurtures. Moses identifies his Lord as the one who gave each thing its creation and then guided it, making care both fitting and directing. | terra: “Our Lord is He who gave each thing its form and then guided it” states the source definition of Rabb as forming something stage by stage toward fitness.
terra: The earth is made serviceable, water descends, and diverse plants emerge, showing the Lord fitting ground and provision together.
terra: Humans and cattle eat the growth, making the field's yield provision and a sign for people of understanding.
terra: Mountains are left as a level plain, recalling the source dictionary's level ground, though this eschatological surface is not cultivated soil.
terra: No crookedness or unevenness is seen in that plain, a precise shape parallel to the level-soil definition but in a different context.

luna: The section connects a nurturing Lord with land revived after rain. This ayah joins human formation through stages to barren earth stirred by water and growing every kind; both images make gradual formation visible. | terra: Human formation through successive stages is paired with barren earth that stirs, swells, and grows after rain, uniting both senses of gradual nurture.
terra: The ayah literally places an extended means or rope beside an act of cutting it; the rhetorical context is different, so this is only an uncertain visual echo of the section's cut cord.
terra: Water makes earth green, and the ayah closes by calling God subtle and خَبِير, joining the field to the divine knower in 100:11.
terra: God subjects what is on earth and the ships, and restrains the sky from falling, a sustained picture of the Lord's preserving care.
terra: The One who gives life, death, and life again is answered by a human described as deeply ungrateful.

luna: The section’s ر ب ب dictionary gloss defines nurturing as bringing something along state by state toward completion. This ayah begins the human’s created stages from an extract of clay, a bodily parallel to that gradual making. | terra: Human creation begins from an extract of clay, opening a staged formation that parallels growth from prepared earth.

luna: The section describes nurturing as a process moving through successive states. This ayah places the human drop in a secure resting place, continuing the bodily sequence from the prior verse. | terra: The human is then placed as a drop in a secure lodging, one distinct stage in gradual nurture.

luna: The section’s dictionary definition of التربية is creation state by state toward completion. This ayah names successive stages of human formation and their final creation; it makes that sense of nurture explicit. | terra: Drop, clot, tissue, bones, flesh, and a new creation are formed in sequence, an especially full Quranic enactment of development حالًا فحالًا toward completion.

luna: The section’s dictionary glosses for ن ق ع and خ ب ر describe water gathered and retained in low earth. This ayah says water is sent down in measure and lodged in earth, while God can take it away; it sharpens both gathering and dependence. | terra: Water descends in due measure and is lodged in the earth, while God can remove it; this closely matches water collected and held in the section's low soil.

luna: The section describes a farmer and the grain promised by good soil. This ayah names gardens of date palms and grapes, abundant fruit, and food from them; it gives the cultivated yield a concrete form. | terra: By the measured water lodged in earth in 23:18, God produces palm and grape gardens with abundant fruit for people to eat.
terra: A tree from Sinai produces oil and food, adding a particular cultivated yield to the watered gardens of 23:19.

luna: The section calls human beings ungrateful to their Rabb despite what they receive. This ayah names hearing, sight, and hearts given by God, followed by the observation that people give little thanks. | terra: God produces people and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, but little gratitude follows, directly pairing formative gifts with failed return.

luna: The section connects testimony with known human conduct. This ayah says tongues, hands, and feet testify against people for what they used to do, making the witness physical and specific. | terra: Tongues, hands, and feet testify to what people did, another resurrection scene in which a person cannot escape witness to conduct.
terra: God drives clouds, joins them, and piles them until rain emerges, expanding the section's cloud as the agent of plant nurture.
terra: The sovereign creator owns heaven and earth, creates everything, and determines it precisely, combining ownership with measured formation.

luna: The section’s field scene begins with wind and rain as provision. This ayah names the winds as glad tidings before mercy and the water sent down from heaven, showing the gift arriving before the land’s yield. | terra: Winds arrive as good tidings before mercy and pure water descends, beginning the same cloud-to-earth care sequence.

luna: The section says water and soil can nourish what becomes a crop. This ayah explains that the rain gives life to a dead land and provides drink for cattle and people; it extends the field’s yield to living recipients. | terra: The water revives dead land and gives drink to creatures, identifying rain as distributed nurture.
terra: The water is repeatedly presented so people may remember, yet most respond only with ingratitude; rain and kenud meet explicitly.
terra: People are asked to look at how many noble pairs God caused earth to grow, a direct appeal to cultivated evidence.
terra: The earth's diverse growth is called a sign, yet most people do not believe, connecting visible nurture with failed recognition.
terra: Pharaoh asks whether “we raised you among us as a child,” using نُرَبِّكَ for nurture while falsely occupying the benefactor's place.
terra: Pharaoh follows his claim of nurture by calling Moses one of the ungrateful, a distorted human version of benefactor accusing recipient that clarifies true lordship by reversal.
terra: Abraham excludes the Lord of the worlds from the objects he calls enemies, separating the true Rabb from false claimants before listing His care.
terra: The Lord of 26:77 is the One who created Abraham and guides him, the first stage of the care that defines true lordship.
terra: He is the One who feeds and gives drink, making ordinary provision an ongoing act of the Rabb.
terra: When Abraham is ill, the Lord heals him, extending nurture from provision to restoration.

luna: The section describes gifts whose source the recipient forgets. Solomon identifies an extraordinary gift as a trial of whether he will be grateful or ungrateful, giving a clear model of recognizing the giver. | terra: Solomon calls the gift “the bounty of my Lord” and a test of gratitude or ingratitude, then says his Lord is self-sufficient and generous.

luna: The section’s Rab dictionary gloss describes the one who nurtures, while its field scene moves from rain to gardens. This ayah asks who sends water and grows gardens whose trees people cannot grow; it locates the harvest’s source beyond the farmer. | terra: God sends water and grows splendid gardens whose trees people could not grow, then asks whether another deity stands with Him; cultivation exposes the true giver.

luna: The section says the human forgets the Rabb behind his gifts. This ayah says the Lord has bounty toward people but most do not give thanks, a direct formulation of the section’s central relation.
terra: After helping others at the well, Moses tells his Lord that he is in need of whatever خَيْر He sends, recognizing good as a gift from its giver.
terra: Towns that exulted in their livelihood were destroyed and left scarcely inhabited, showing provision enjoyed without a sustaining relation to its giver.
terra: Night and day are made for rest and seeking bounty so that people may give thanks, explicitly directing provision back toward gratitude.
terra: Qarun's immense treasures make him exult, beginning the case of a recipient whose possession obscures its giver.
terra: The command “do good as God has done good to you” states the onward flow of received bounty and forbids corrupting the earth.
terra: Qarun credits his wealth to his own knowledge, forgetting that it was received and reproducing the section's love of gift without giver.
terra: Those desiring the nearer life wish for Qarun's fortune, illustrating love fixed on the visible gift.
terra: Those given knowledge say God's reward is better, placing a durable good against fascination with Qarun's wealth.
terra: God causes earth to swallow Qarun and his dwelling, showing that possessed goods cannot protect their owner from the giver's command.
terra: After Qarun is swallowed, former admirers recognize that God expands and restricts provision and that His grace spared them, correcting their earlier fixation on the gift.
terra: People are commanded to seek provision from God, worship Him, and thank Him, laying out giver, gift, and return in one ayah.
terra: Many creatures cannot carry their provision, yet God provides for them and for people, emphasizing continuing dependence on the giver.

luna: The section’s field chain joins rain, revived land, and the human response to the giver. This ayah asks who sends water and revives earth after death; the answer is God, while most people fail to understand, joining recognition to the scene. | terra: Even those asked who sends rain and revives earth say “Allah,” yet most do not understand; verbal recognition has not become a full response.

luna: The section names the human’s ingratitude to the Rabb. This ayah says people call on God sincerely aboard a ship but associate others with Him once safely brought to land, matching the rescue-and-turning pattern. | terra: Those in a ship call God with exclusive devotion, supplying the moment when danger reveals the giver.
terra: After rescue they deny what God gave them, the cut return that completes the scene of 29:65.

luna: The section builds a field image from rain and land. This ayah names rain from the sky that revives the earth after its death among God’s signs, showing how the yield can call the recipient to recognize its source.

luna: The section’s image joins distress and remembered care. This ayah says people call on their Lord when harm touches them, even though the resulting response to mercy is described in 30:34; this row contributes the appeal. | terra: Distress makes people call their Lord in repentance, but tasted mercy then leads a faction to associate partners with Him.

luna: The section says people fail to return thanks for gifts. This ayah says some associate partners after God lets them taste mercy; 30:33 supplies the distress-and-appeal preceding this row. | terra: Their association is described as ingratitude for what God gave, making the severed relation in 30:33 explicit.
terra: Usury given to grow through people's wealth does not grow with God, while alms seeking God's face are multiplied; apparent gain and true generous growth are reversed.
terra: Winds are sent as good tidings and means to seek God's bounty so that people may be grateful, joining wind, gift, and return.

luna: The section’s root ث و ر glosses the wind’s action as raising clouds; this ayah says the winds stir up سحاب and the clouds bring rain. The verbal and weather scene shows the first link in the nurturing chain. | terra: The wind raises cloud with the exact secondary action فَتُثِيرُ سَحَابًا named from the source section, then rain issues from it.

luna: The section’s field depends on a Rabb who raises life through stages. This ayah directs attention to God’s mercy in reviving earth after its death; the dead-to-living contrast shows what the nurturing relation can bring about. | terra: The effects of God's mercy are seen in earth revived after death, inviting attention to the giver behind growth.
terra: Water sent from the sky grows every noble kind on earth, a direct rain-to-soil parallel.
terra: After the rain-grown creatures of 31:10, God calls this His creation and challenges people to show what others created, restoring the maker behind the scene.

luna: The section depicts ingratitude as failing to answer a gift. Luqman is given wisdom and told to give thanks; the ayah adds that gratitude benefits the grateful person, clarifying the relation’s consequence. | terra: Wisdom is framed as gratitude; whoever thanks benefits himself, while the ungrateful cannot diminish the self-sufficient, praiseworthy giver.
terra: Maternal weakness and nursing are followed by the command to thank God and one's parents, joining sustained nurture with reciprocal gratitude.
terra: Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought forth by God, who is subtle and خَبِير; nothing buried escapes the Rabb's knowledge.
terra: Submitting oneself to God while doing good is described as grasping the firmest handhold, the maintained relation opposite kenud severance.
terra: Ships move by God's favor so that He may show His signs, which are recognized by every steadfast, grateful person.
terra: People in engulfing waves call God sincerely, yet after rescue some only partly fulfill the return; the ayah ends by naming treacherous ingratitude.
terra: After proportioning the human, God gives spirit, hearing, sight, and hearts, yet little thanks is given; completed formation meets failed return.
terra: Water is driven to barren land and produces crops eaten by livestock and people, closely reversing earth that grows nothing despite care.

luna: The section says gratitude is the response to provision but easily withheld. Solomon’s household is told to work in gratitude, and the verse says few servants are grateful; it makes gratitude a practical return for gifts. | terra: David's family is commanded to work in gratitude, and few servants are called truly grateful; gratitude is sustained action rather than mere possession of gifts.

luna: The section’s field image joins land, provision, and the human response of thanks. This ayah describes Sheba’s two gardens and tells them to eat their Lord’s provision and give thanks; it makes the reciprocity explicit. | terra: A good land with two gardens is explicitly paired with “eat of your Lord's provision and thank Him,” the productive answer to the section's rain and care.

luna: The section describes water as a condition of fruitful land. This ayah says a flood was sent upon Sheba and their two gardens were replaced by bitter-fruited ones; water and land turn from provision to loss. | terra: When the people turn away, the flood of the dam replaces their two gardens with bitter, sparse growth; severed gratitude becomes ruined earth.

luna: The section calls human ingratitude a failure to answer provision. This ayah identifies the people’s kufr as the reason for recompense after the garden account, making the field’s failure a moral boundary as well. | terra: The ruined gardens are called a recompense for ingratitude, making explicit what the flood-and-field reversal in 34:16 means.

luna: The section says gifts are completed by the Rabb and can be met with gratitude. This ayah says whatever people spend, God replaces it and is the best provider, making provision and return a continuing relation.

luna: The section says a person forgets the Rabb who provides and nurtures. This ayah asks people to remember God’s favor and asks who provides from heaven and earth, directing attention from provision back to its giver.

luna: The section links wind, cloud, rain, and a dead field. This ayah describes God sending winds that stir clouds and driving them to a dead land, then reviving the earth; it closely restages that sequence. | terra: Winds تُثِيرُ سَحَابًا and the cloud revives dead land, joining the section's exact wind-cloud wording to earth made productive.
terra: Fresh and salt seas yield food and ornament, while ships cross so people may seek God's bounty and perhaps give thanks.
terra: Water from the sky brings fruits of varied colors, a direct repetition of the cloud-to-yield part of the image.

luna: The section says the Rabb is fully informed of people and names the contents of the chest. This ayah says God knows the unseen of the heavens and earth and what breasts conceal, directly connecting hiddenness and knowledge.

luna: The section develops kenūd land as soil that produces nothing. This ayah points to dead earth revived and grain brought out for people to eat, making the contrast between withheld and yielded nourishment visible. | terra: God revives dead earth and brings grain, حَبًّا, from it; the source section explicitly hears this grain beside حُبّ in 100:8.
terra: Gardens and flowing springs complete the watered field introduced in 36:33.
terra: People eat the field's fruit although their hands did not create it, and are asked whether they will thank; gift, labor, and return meet explicitly.

luna: The section says the human’s testimony may be directed against himself. This ayah says hands speak and feet testify to what people earned, a bodily disclosure of the actions at issue. | terra: On the day of disclosure, mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to earnings, concretizing the human's unavoidable witness to his own conduct.
terra: The human sees that God created him from a drop yet becomes an open adversary, turning formative care into opposition.
terra: The human offers a challenge about revived bones while forgetting his own creation, an exact case of forgetting prior nurture.
terra: The answer points back to the One who produced creation the first time and knows every creation, restoring maker and knowledge together.
terra: Fine standing horses are presented to Solomon, supplying the concrete al-khayr whose love he names in 38:32.
terra: Solomon says he loved the love of al-khayr over remembrance of his Lord, a close verbal meeting with حُبِّ ٱلْخَيْرِ and forgetting the giver.
terra: People are created in their mothers through successive creations in three darknesses, then the ayah identifies this maker as Allah their Lord and sovereign.
terra: God needs no one and is not pleased with ingratitude, but approves gratitude, defining the receiver's two stances without making the giver dependent on the return.

luna: The section says a person forgets gifts and cuts the return of gratitude. This ayah says that after God removes distress and grants favor, the person forgets the plea and assigns partners; it states the severance plainly. | terra: In harm the human turns to his Lord, then after being granted favor forgets the One previously invoked; it is an exact ease-after-affliction enactment of kenud.

luna: The section’s dictionary senses include water gathered in low earth and a farmer working soil. This ayah describes rain entering springs, crops growing, then yellowing and becoming debris; it shows both nourishing growth and its passing. | terra: Water descends, enters the earth as springs, and brings crops through stages before they dry, matching collected water and gradual completion while marking growth's limit.

luna: The section says the human loves what he receives but forgets its giver. This ayah says that after favor reaches him, he claims it came through his own knowledge, a specific way of obscuring the Rabb’s hand. | terra: When harm touches the human he calls God, but after favor he credits his own knowledge; the gift remains while its giver is erased.
luna: The section says that on the day of reckoning the Rabb remains fully informed. This ayah shows the earth illuminated, the record set down, and witnesses brought, a direct scene of judgment.

luna: The section’s 100:11 says the Rabb is fully informed of people on that day. This ayah says every soul is repaid for what it did and God knows best what they do, joining knowledge to just recompense.
terra: God shows signs and sends provision from the sky, yet only one who turns back remembers, linking descent of provision to remembered giver.

luna: The section sees ordinary care as a gift whose source is forgotten. This ayah names night for rest and day for sight, then says most people do not give thanks for God’s favor. | terra: Night is made for rest and day for sight, yet most people do not thank despite God's bounty to them.
terra: God makes earth a settled place, forms people well, and provides good things, then identifies Himself as their Lord; ownership, fitting, and completed benefit meet.
terra: Because the living God is Lord of the worlds, people are commanded to call on Him sincerely and praise Him after the provisions listed in 40:64.
terra: Creation from dust, drop, and clot proceeds through childhood, maturity, and old age, directly presenting the Lord's stage-by-stage formation.
terra: God blesses earth and apportions its sustenance in measured days, presenting the field as fitted and provisioned rather than self-producing.

luna: The section allows the human to be witness to his own ingratitude. This ayah says people’s hearing, sight, and skins testify against them, supplying bodily witnesses to deeds. | terra: Hearing, sight, and skins testify against their owners, giving bodily form to testimony over denied conduct.
terra: The skins answer that the God who gives all speech made them speak, locating their testimony under divine power rather than voluntary confession.
terra: The offenders did not expect their faculties to testify and supposed God did not know much of what they did, exactly opposing the Rabb whose knowledge cannot be escaped.
terra: Their supposition about their Lord ruins them, showing that severing acknowledgment never places them outside His knowledge.

luna: The section describes a field whose soil may fail to yield. This ayah shows dry earth stirred by rain until it swells and produces, a vivid reversal from lifelessness to growth. | terra: Humbled earth stirs and swells when water descends; the same giver who revives it will revive the dead.

luna: The section sets the human’s intense love of خير against his attention to calamity. This ayah says the person does not tire of asking for good but despairs when evil touches him, a direct imbalance in what is remembered. | terra: The human never tires of asking for ٱلْخَيْرِ but becomes despairing when evil touches him, using the named word in a broader “good” sense while privileging affliction over bounty.

luna: The section says the human forgets the giver after receiving a gift. This ayah describes a person claiming favor as his own and doubting the Hour; the self-attribution makes ingratitude more than a missed thank-you. | terra: After mercy follows distress, the human says “this is mine,” appropriating a received gift and doubting accountability.

luna: The section describes the human as ungrateful to the one who cares for him. This ayah says that when favor is bestowed he turns away, but when evil touches him he makes lengthy supplication, a reversal in his response to ease and distress. | terra: Favor makes the human turn away, while harm produces prolonged prayer; the two directions display the section's cut return.
terra: The one who seeks the harvest of the Hereafter has that harvest increased, while the seeker of the world's harvest receives only some of it; field yield becomes a measure of chosen good.
terra: If God expanded provision without measure people would transgress; He sends it by measure and is fully aware of His servants, joining calibrated care to خَبِير.

luna: The section links receiving mercy to a failure to answer the Rabb. This ayah says that when people taste mercy they rejoice, but when their own hands have sent ahead evil they become ungrateful; it shows the unstable response to provision. | terra: A tasted mercy makes people rejoice, but an evil earned by their hands exposes the human as ungrateful; the differing responses enact kenud.
terra: Earth is made a resting place with roads for guidance, preparing the measured water and revived land of 43:11.

luna: The section says rain completes care of the land. This ayah says God sends water in measure and revives a dead land with it, joining measured provision to renewed growth. | terra: Measured water descends and revives a dead land, tying calibrated provision to the earth's capacity to yield.
terra: When seated on a means of travel people are instructed to remember their Lord's favor, preserving the giver within enjoyment of the gift.
terra: Despite those created means, the human assigns part of God's servants to Him and is called manifestly ungrateful.

luna: The section places winds and water in the chain of field care. This ayah names winds and rain that revives earth after its death among God’s signs, tying the scene to recognition of the giver. | terra: Provision descends from the sky, revives earth, and accompanies the changing winds, another compact version of the section's field system.
terra: God subjects the sea so ships may travel and people may seek His bounty and perhaps thank, another provision-to-gratitude formulation.

luna: The section says the human will be raised and the Rabb will be fully informed on that day. This ayah depicts every community kneeling and summoned to its record, placing the account in a public judgment scene.
luna: The section says the Rabb knows those who cut the gratitude bond. This ayah presents a truthful record of everything people did, making the knowledge of their acts concrete.
terra: Parental gestation and rearing culminate in a prayer for help to thank God's favor upon child and parents, linking nurture to its proper return.
terra: A cloud approaching the valleys is welcomed as rain, but is identified instead as the hastened punishment; the normally nurturing cloud carries the opposite outcome.
terra: The wind destroys everything by its Lord's command, completing the reversal of the expected raincloud in 46:24.

luna: The section’s dictionary sense of K-N-D includes refusing continuing closeness. This ayah asks whether people will turn away and cut their kinship ties, extending the image of broken connection to family relations. | terra: Turning away is associated with corrupting earth and severing kinship, a direct Quranic instance of refusing to maintain a relation.
terra: Those summoned to spend from received wealth may withhold, but their stinginess harms themselves because God is self-sufficient and they are needy; turning away can bring replacement.
terra: The Prophet's favor is completed and he is guided on a straight path, pairing completion with direction.

luna: The section says people in the graves will be raised and their Lord knows them. This ayah says God knows what the earth consumes of them and has a preserving record, joining the grave to divine knowledge.
terra: Earth is spread, stabilized, and made to grow beautiful pairs before the blessed rain and grain of 50:9.

luna: The section’s field depends on water that nurtures growth. This ayah calls the rain water blessed and says it grows gardens and grain to harvest; it makes the same provision-to-crop movement explicit. | terra: Blessed water produces gardens and grain for harvest, joining rain to the source section's secondary حَبّ image.

luna: The section specifically names the farmer’s yield and grain. This ayah continues the rain-grown scene with tall date palms bearing clustered fruit, giving a particular image of completed growth. | terra: Tall palms with layered clusters specify the mature yield of the blessed water in 50:9.

luna: The section links a land’s yield to nourishment for living beings. This ayah calls the crops provision for servants and says rain revives dead land; the harvest becomes a gift received, not merely a field’s output. | terra: The crop is provision for servants and revives dead land, naming the field's yield as a gift rather than an autonomous product.
terra: The Creator knows what the human soul whispers and is nearer than the jugular vein, directly excluding escape from the Rabb's knowledge.

luna: The section’s witness may be the human or the Rabb, and its final ayah places the reckoning on that day. This ayah says every soul comes with a driver and a witness, making the accountability scene explicit.
luna: The section says what is hidden in chests will be brought to light. This ayah describes the veil being removed and a person’s sight becoming sharp, a concrete image of disclosure on the day.

luna: The section’s خير gloss includes generosity, while its kenūd figure withholds the return. This ayah says a rightful share in wealth belongs to the petitioner and deprived person, making generosity a concrete response to provision.
terra: Heaven's gates open with pouring water, but the abundant descent is judgment rather than plant-nurturing mercy.
terra: Earth bursts with springs and the two waters meet for a decreed matter, a destructive counterpart to water collecting in receptive soil.
terra: The earth is laid out for creatures, preparing the provision named in the following ayat.
terra: Fruit and palms stand on the prepared earth as its received yield.
terra: Grain, ٱلْحَبُّ, and fragrant plants repeat the source section's grain-sense beside the loved “good.”
terra: Immediately after earth, fruit, and grain, humans are asked which favors of their Lord they deny.

luna: The section names the farmer in its root خ ب ر gloss and describes land worked for a crop. This ayah asks whether people have considered what they sow or plow (تحرثون), focusing attention on the human labor in that field. | terra: The question “Have you considered what you till?” places the human farmer inside the section's field.

luna: The section’s farmer works soil that may still be kenūd. This ayah asks whether people make the crop grow or God does, distinguishing cultivation from the power that completes its yield. | terra: God asks whether people make the crop grow or He does, distinguishing the worker of the soil from the Lord who actually nurtures it.
terra: God could make the crop shattered debris; this is the explicit non-yield boundary of the otherwise tended field.
terra: After imagined crop-loss the speakers dwell on the cost they incurred, illustrating the kenud focus on misfortune; its meaning depends on the ruined field in 56:65.
terra: Their conclusion “we are deprived” completes the loss-counting response to the failed harvest of 56:65.

luna: The section’s field imagery treats water as a gift needed for growth. This ayah asks people to consider the water they drink, opening the passage that questions its source. | terra: The water people drink is called to attention as part of the gift-chain that makes their field possible.

luna: The section names clouds and rain as part of the field’s care. This ayah asks whether people bring drinking water down from the rain clouds or God does, placing the source beyond the recipient. | terra: God asks whether people send water from the raincloud or He does, identifying the cloud's nurturing agency with its giver.

luna: The section places rainfall among the gifts that call for thanks. After asking about water from rain clouds in 56:68–69, this ayah says God could make it bitter and asks why they do not give thanks; it makes water’s dependence and the proper return explicit. | terra: God could make the water bitter and therefore asks why people do not give thanks; usable rain and gratitude are joined directly.
terra: The sequence of crop, water, and other provisions concludes by commanding glorification of the great Lord's name.

luna: The section describes people receiving good and cutting off thanks. This ayah asks whether they make their provision an act of denial, explicitly turning provision into the point at which gratitude is withheld.
terra: People are told to spend from that over which God made them successors, making generosity a continuation of property first entrusted to them.
terra: Hearts are warned not to harden against God's remembrance immediately before 57:17 says He revives dead earth, making receptivity the bridge between person and soil.
terra: God revives earth after its death immediately after warning against hardened hearts, inviting the responsive human to be read through receptive soil.
terra: Rain-produced growth pleases its cultivators and then withers, using the farmer's gaze to show that even successful yield is not self-sustaining.

luna: The section says the human forgets favors while the Rabb remains fully informed. This ayah says God will inform people of what they did, which He counted while they forgot, making the contrast between human forgetting and divine knowledge exact. | terra: God has enumerated deeds that people forgot and will inform them of those deeds, then is called witness over everything; counting, forgetting, knowledge, and testimony converge.
terra: Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract from remembrance of God, the precise boundary between loving gifts and forgetting their giver.
terra: People are commanded to spend from what God provided before death makes them beg for delay to give, treating provision as something meant to continue onward.

luna: The section says the Rabb is fully informed of people on that day. This ayah says God knows what is in the heavens and earth and what people conceal or declare, connecting hidden contents with divine knowledge. | terra: God knows what is concealed and disclosed and what breasts contain, closely matching the Lord informed of the contents brought out from within.

luna: The section says the Rabb knows those who act as though their ingratitude can be hidden. This ayah says God knows what is concealed in breasts as well as what is declared, extending the image inward. | terra: Whether speech is concealed or declared, God knows what is within breasts, paralleling the hidden contents gathered before the knowing Lord in 100:10-11.

luna: The section calls the Lord خبير, fully informed. This ayah asks whether the One who created would not know, and calls Him لطيف خبير; it links creating and knowing the inward person. | terra: The Creator necessarily knows what He formed and is called خَبِير, linking nurture, ownership, and complete knowledge.
terra: Earth is made manageable for people to traverse and eat from God's provision, joining prepared ground to received livelihood.
terra: The Creator who produced people and gave hearing, sight, and hearts receives little gratitude, concisely matching nurture and kenud.
luna: The section’s low-land gloss describes rainwater gathering in earth. This ayah asks who could bring flowing water if it sank away, making dependence on retained water explicit.

luna: The section’s field image makes a yield-bearing garden a sign of care and response. This ayah itself frames the owners’ garden as a test; 68:24 later supplies their decision to bar the poor, so this row contributes the garden-as-test setting. | terra: The garden owners are tested through the crop they presume they can harvest, making cultivated bounty itself the site of their response.
terra: The garden owners make no exception in their oath; this plausibly marks presumed control over bounty, including the remembered reading that they omitted “if God wills.”
terra: A visitation from their Lord circles the garden while they sleep; the giver can withhold the growth the owners treated as theirs alone.
terra: The garden becomes as if harvested bare, a vivid counterpart to land that gives nothing.

luna: The section’s K-N-D gloss includes cutting a continuing relation. In this garden parable, the owners whisper that no poor person should enter, showing a crop’s recipients deliberately cut out of its yield. | terra: The owners agree that no poor person will enter the garden, cutting the onward path by which the received bounty should become generosity.
terra: They proceed intending deprivation while imagining themselves capable, combining control of the field with refusal to give.
terra: On seeing the ruined field they conclude that they are deprived, counting their loss after they had planned others' deprivation.
terra: The most balanced among them recalls that he urged them to glorify God, naming the response to bounty they omitted.

luna: The section asks a receiver to recognize the Rabb behind provision. After the garden is lost, the owners say “سبحان ربنا” and admit wrongdoing; their recognition makes explicit what the ingrate failed to acknowledge. | terra: They finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, restoring in speech the giver whom their plan had excluded.
terra: They hope their Lord will replace the garden with something better and turn toward Him, explicitly reattaching field and giver.

luna: The section says no one escapes the Rabb’s knowledge on that day. This ayah says people will be exposed and none of their secrets will remain hidden, directly matching the disclosure of inward contents.
terra: The human is described as anxiously unstable, introducing the two unequal responses to harm and good in 70:20-21.

luna: The section says the kenūd person counts calamities. This ayah describes the human as distressed when touched by evil, one side of a response that measures what is lost. | terra: When evil touches him he is frantic, the adversity-counting side of the kenud disposition.

luna: The section says the kenūd person forgets blessings. This ayah says the human withholds when good touches him, showing how receiving a gift can end in non-return. | terra: When ٱلْخَيْرُ touches him he withholds it, using the named word for received good that neither becomes gratitude nor continues onward.
luna: The section’s human loves خير but may fail to return it. This ayah describes a known share in the wealth of the people who pray, giving a specific form to generosity.

luna: The section’s K-N-D gloss includes neglecting what should be returned. This ayah identifies the recipients of that share as the petitioner and deprived person, specifying who the generous response reaches.

luna: The section asks the recipient to acknowledge the Rabb behind provision. This ayah contributes the call to seek forgiveness; 71:11 supplies the promised rain, so the adjacent verses connect a return to God with renewed provision.

luna: The section pictures rain completing the care of a field. This ayah promises abundant rain in response to seeking forgiveness, showing provision arriving from above. | terra: The sky is promised as abundant rain in response to turning back, beginning a renewed chain of nurture.

luna: The section connects divine care with fertile ground. This ayah continues the promise with wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, laying out a full scene of gifts that could be acknowledged. | terra: Rain becomes wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, unfolding the completed favors for which the surrounding address asks recognition.

luna: The section places Rabb before the charge of ingratitude. This ayah asks why people do not attribute due greatness to God, directly addressing the failure to honor the one named as Rabb. | terra: The people are asked why they do not expect due greatness from God after the gifts of 71:11-12.

luna: The section’s root ر ب ب gloss describes bringing something through successive states to completion. This ayah says God created people in stages (أطوارا), a concise parallel to that dictionary sense. | terra: God created people in successive stages, a direct formulation of the section's حالًا فحالًا account of nurture.
terra: God is said to have caused people to grow from earth as a growth, applying the section's plant image directly to divine nurture of humanity.
terra: God returns people to earth and will bring them out again, completing the human-as-growth image of 71:17.
terra: Steadfastness on the way would be met with abundant water as a test, making gathered water both provision and a measure of response.
terra: The abundant water of 72:16 tests people, while turning from remembrance of one's Lord leads elsewhere; gift and forgotten Rabb form the fork.

luna: The section’s surah context says what is in the chests will be brought to light. This ayah says the human will be informed of what he sent ahead and left behind, specifying what the reckoning reveals.

luna: The section says the human may be the witness in 100:7. This ayah says a person is a witness against himself, directly supporting that reading of the pronoun. | terra: The human is a witness against himself even while offering excuses, supporting the human referent of “he is witness to that” in 100:7.
luna: The section frames witness as knowledge that cannot be cut away by denial. This ayah says a person’s excuses do not erase that self-witness, extending the accountability in 75:14.
terra: The human once passed through a period when he was not a mentioned thing, framing the created dependence specified in 76:2.
terra: God creates the human from a mixed drop for testing and gives hearing and sight, supplying the care to which 76:3 says gratitude or ingratitude answers.

luna: The section sets the gift of care against kenūd ingratitude. This ayah says the way was shown, then names the two responses as شاكرا or كفورا; it makes the severed bond a chosen response. | terra: After being shown the way, the human may be grateful or ungrateful; the ayah states the two possible returns to divine guidance.

luna: The section says خير includes generosity and a gift’s proper response. This ayah describes feeding the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, turning attachment into generous giving.

luna: The section asks what connects a recipient to the giver after provision. This ayah says the givers act only for God’s sake and seek neither repayment nor thanks, clarifying the motive that kenūd lacks. | terra: The righteous giver seeks neither repayment nor thanks from the people fed, setting a boundary: human generosity should not demand the reciprocal gratitude owed to God.
terra: Creation from a humble fluid begins a compact sequence of measured formation.
terra: The fluid is placed in a secure lodging, showing protective nurture within the sequence.
terra: The lodging holds it for a known term, adding duration and measure to formation.
terra: God declares that He determined the process and is the best determiner, closing the staged womb scene with calibrated care.

luna: The section names clouds that nourish plants and rain that reaches the ground. This ayah describes abundant water poured from rain clouds, the direct source of the field’s growth. | terra: Abundant pouring water descends from rainclouds, initiating a compact field sequence.

luna: The section names grain as the expected yield from cared-for soil. This ayah connects rain to the production of grain and plants, giving the scene’s hoped-for harvest. | terra: The water brings forth grain and vegetation, again meeting the section's حَبّ sense.

luna: The section’s farmer works for a yield from the land. This ayah adds thick gardens to the rain-fed scene, a visible instance of soil that does produce. | terra: Dense gardens complete the rain-to-growth sequence of 78:14-15.
terra: Pharaoh's claim “I am your highest lord” is the extreme false appropriation of ownership and mastery.
terra: Earth's water and pasture are brought out, describing provision emerging from prepared ground.
terra: The water and pasture are called provision for humans and cattle, identifying the yield's beneficiaries.
terra: The human is denounced for extreme ingratitude before his formation and food are unfolded, making the following care the measure of the charge.
terra: A question directs the ungrateful human back to the material from which God created him.
terra: Creation from a drop is followed by proportioning, one explicit stage in the Rabb's gradual formation.
terra: God then makes the human's way easy, continuing the sequence of fitted care.
terra: Death and burial remain under the same giver's ordering, so dependence is not ended by imagined self-sufficiency.
terra: God raises the human when He wills, completing the staged history that begins in 80:19.
terra: Between staged creation and the command to inspect food, the human is said not yet to have fulfilled what God commanded, naming failed response to the surrounding care.

luna: The section turns on what the earth produces under care. This ayah itself asks the human to look at his food; 80:25 supplies the rain-and-soil sequence, so this row contributes the question that directs attention to the source of food. | terra: The human is commanded to look at his food, shifting the charge of ingratitude into inspection of provision.

luna: The section describes a farmer working soil and awaiting its yield. This ayah says water is poured down abundantly before the earth is split, presenting the first physical steps toward the crop. | terra: God pours water abundantly, the first step in the food's cultivation.

luna: The section’s grain image is developed here: after water, the earth is split open. This ayah gives the ground’s opening as the immediate scene that makes growth possible. | terra: God splits the earth open, making the soil receptive to that water.

luna: The section explicitly names the grain حبة in wheat and barley. This ayah names grain among the foods brought out of the earth, joining the dictionary detail to a crop scene. | terra: Grain, حَبًّا, is grown in the opened earth, exactly supplying the section's secondary grain image.

luna: The section expects a fruitful field after rain. This ayah adds grapes and fodder to the earth’s yield, showing that the provision extends beyond grain. | terra: Grapes and herbage add to the yield of the watered soil.

luna: The section names the farmer and the crop-bearing land. This ayah names olives and palms among the yield, making the cared-for field visible as a varied orchard. | terra: Olives and palms extend the cultivated provision.
